New Jersey property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Any owner may appeal an assessment to the County Board of Taxation; for assessments over $1,000,000 the owner may instead file directly with the Tax Court of New Jersey. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • Petitions to the county board or Tax Court must be filed and received on or before April 1; where a municipal revaluation or reassessment occurred, the deadline is May 1. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties use an alternative assessment calendar with a January 15 appeal deadline. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • To be excessive or discriminatory, an assessment must be shown not to fairly represent the True Market Value Standard or the Common Level Range Standard; the common level range is plus or minus 15% of the district's average ratio. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • Appeal is made by filing Form A-1 and Form A-1 Comp. Sale with the County Board of Taxation. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • From a county board judgment, an appeal to the Tax Court must be filed within 45 days of the judgment date. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • The Director's Ratio (Average Ratio Assessed to True Value) is published in the Table of Equalized Valuations certified on or before October 1 each year. (NJ Division of Taxation - Realty Transfer Fees FAQ; source)
  • All 566 municipalities must hold at least one tax sale per year if there are delinquent taxes or municipal charges. (Elements of Tax Sales in New Jersey | NJ DCA Division of Local Government Services; source)
  • Winning bidder is the one bidding the lowest percentage of interest (bid down from up to 18%) or, at 0-1%, the highest premium. (Elements of Tax Sales in New Jersey | NJ DCA Division of Local Government Services; source)

What the official sources say

  • State relief programs for homeowners are the Senior Freeze (Property Tax Reimbursement), ANCHOR and Stay NJ; eligibility and income limits are subject to appropriation by the State Budget. (Property Tax Relief Programs FAQs | NJ Division of Taxation; source)
  • ANCHOR homeowners: NJ residents who own and occupy a home as of October 1, 2025 with gross income up to $250,000 (renters up to $150,000). (Property Tax Relief Programs FAQs | NJ Division of Taxation; source)
  • Stay NJ: homeowners aged 65 or older who own and occupy the home as principal residence for the entire year; FY2027 budget provides payments in 2027 for incomes up to $200,000. (Property Tax Relief Programs FAQs | NJ Division of Taxation; source)
  • Senior Freeze: homeowners born in 1960 or earlier, or actually receiving Social Security/Railroad Retirement disability benefits, who meet eligibility requirements. (Property Tax Relief Programs FAQs | NJ Division of Taxation; source)
  • Benefits apply to the qualifying property owned/occupied on October 1 (ANCHOR); total relief cannot exceed property taxes paid on the principal residence. (Property Tax Relief Programs FAQs | NJ Division of Taxation; source)
  • Homeowners who sell and move must indicate the move on the Homestead Benefit application or take credit at closing; otherwise the credit may go to the new owners' taxes. (Buying or Selling a Home in New Jersey | NJ Division of Taxation tax guide; source)

Does New Jersey have a homestead exemption?

People searching for a New Jersey homestead exemption usually end up at the state's property tax relief programs. The Division of Taxation runs three of them for homeowners: Senior Freeze (Property Tax Reimbursement), ANCHOR and Stay NJ, all filed on one combined application called the PAS-1. Municipalities add their own deductions on top.

The programs pay benefits to qualifying owners and are tied to a principal residence and to income. The state's own FAQ says eligibility rules, income limits and benefit amounts for each program depend on appropriation in the State Budget, so they can shift from year to year.

The application for 2025 closed on November 2, 2026, per the Division of Taxation. Anyone who missed it should look at what the next filing season brings on the Division's relief page.

Which New Jersey property tax relief program fits which homeowner?

The three programs overlap, and the Division decides which benefits an applicant gets. The table compares them using the Division's published rules.

NJ Division of Taxation property tax relief programs, 2025 application year
ProgramWho qualifiesIncome limit
ANCHORHomeowners who owned and occupied the home on October 1, 2025, and renters$250,000 for homeowners, $150,000 for renters
Senior FreezeAge 65 or older, or receiving Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability, and owned and lived in the home since December 31, 2022 or earlier$172,475 for 2025
Stay NJHomeowners 65 or older who owned and lived in the home all 12 months of 2025$200,000 or less

A homeowner under 65 who does not receive Social Security disability can only qualify for ANCHOR, according to the FAQ. A homeowner who is 65 or older may qualify for all three.

How much does Stay NJ pay?

The Division's Stay NJ page ties the maximum to income. For the 2027 payments covering the 2025 tax year, the maximum benefit is $6,500 at income up to $100,000, $5,000 above that through $150,000, and $4,000 above that through $200,000. Over $200,000 the benefit is zero.

Payments come in quarterly installments. The Division says the 2025 benefit is paid in February and May of 2027, and the remainder of the earlier 2024 benefit was split between August and November 2026. Each applicant gets a benefit statement that lists Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ amounts.

The FAQ sets one cap that applies to all three: total relief cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the principal residence for the qualifying year. Property tax relief payments are not taxable income for New Jersey state taxes.

What property and ownership rules apply?

The home must be the applicant's principal residence. The FAQ defines that as the place you live most of the time and where you vote or get mail, and for owners it is the property on the deed or tax records. A vacation home, a second home or a rental property does not qualify.

  • Senior Freeze: not available on property with more than four units, or with four units or fewer that contains more than one commercial unit, and not available if you make P.I.L.O.T. payments instead of property tax.
  • Stay NJ: mobile homeowners and renters are excluded, a co-owned home is calculated on your ownership percentage, and a duplex is calculated on the share of the property you occupy.
  • Trusts and life estates: a trust beneficiary, or someone with a life estate or a 99-year lease, can qualify and must send the trust, deed or lease document.

Condominium owners and resident co-op shareholders who pay property tax on their unit count as homeowners, the relief page says.

What local New Jersey property tax deductions exist?

Municipalities handle several deductions and exemptions directly. The Division of Taxation lists a $250 deduction for senior citizens and disabled persons, a $250 veteran deduction, and a 100 percent exemption for disabled veterans.

The senior and disabled deduction has its own tests in the Division's brochure. The owner must be 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, or an unmarried surviving spouse age 55 or older of such a person. The owner must have lived in New Jersey for a year as of October 1 before the deduction year, owned and lived in the dwelling on that date, and kept income to $10,000 or less with certain exclusions such as Social Security. Form PTD is filed with the municipal assessor or collector, followed by a yearly income statement.

For the veteran programs and the exact forms, ask the local tax assessor. These deductions come through the town, not through the state application.

What happens to relief benefits if I sell or move?

The ANCHOR FAQ says a homeowner who moved during the year is still eligible, but the benefit follows the qualifying property owned and occupied on October 1. A divorced or separated applicant follows the same test: whoever owned and occupied the home on October 1 may apply.

The Division's older seller guide covers the closing side. It says that when a benefit check is processed after a move has been properly shown on the application, the money goes to the seller. If the move is not shown, the seller needs to take credit for the benefit at closing, and if the seller, an attorney or the closing agent misses it, the credit lands on the new owners' taxes. That guide describes the Homestead Benefit, the earlier program, so ask the title company how current benefits are being handled for your closing.

Senior Freeze recipients who buy another New Jersey home must re-establish eligibility for the new property. The guide says a seller who received a reimbursement the year before moving waits two years for a new base year instead of the standard three, then files Form PTR-1-C.

What other tax breaks matter when selling a New Jersey home?

The same Division guide lists the main items a New Jersey seller meets at closing. Sales tax is not due on a home sale, and the seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee of 1 percent under the guide's summary. Every seller furnishes a GIT/REP form to record the deed, and New Jersey residents use GIT/REP-3 to avoid an estimated income tax payment at closing.

A seller who qualifies for the federal principal residence exclusion can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, after owning and living in the home two of the last five years. Nonresident sellers face an estimated payment of 2 percent of the sale price or 8.97 percent of net gain unless an exemption applies.

The Division's realty fee page shows the transfer fee is figured per $500 of consideration, with rates that step up as the price rises and an extra Graduated Percent Fee on residential sales above $1,000,000.

More questions about New Jersey Homestead Exemption

Is there a New Jersey homestead exemption that lowers my assessed value?

No single program works that way. New Jersey offers ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ as payments through the state, plus local deductions such as the $250 senior and disabled deduction handled by your municipality.

Who qualifies for ANCHOR as a homeowner?

A New Jersey resident who owned and lived in the home on October 1, 2025, with gross income up to $250,000. Renters qualify with income up to $150,000. The home must be the principal residence.

Can I get Stay NJ if I am under 65?

No. The Division says you or your spouse must have been 65 or older in 2025, and receiving Social Security disability does not change that. Mobile homeowners and renters are also excluded.

What if I sold my house after filing the property tax relief application?

The benefit follows the home you owned and occupied on October 1. Show the move on the application, or take credit at closing as the state's seller guide describes, so the benefit does not pass to the new owners.

Do property tax relief payments count as taxable income in New Jersey?

No. The Division of Taxation FAQ says relief payments are not taxable income for New Jersey state taxes. Each applicant's total benefits also cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the home.

New Jersey Real Estate Transfer Tax: Rates, Exemptions and Who Pays

Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Jersey Real Estate Transfer Tax sale
  • Turn the New Jersey Real Estate Transfer Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Graduated Percent Fee ('mansion tax') on consideration over $1,000,000 for Class 2 residential and certain other classes: 1% over $1M to $2M, 2% over $2M to $2.5M, 2.5% to $3M, 3% to $3.5M, 3.5% above $3.5M; the RTF page says the seller is statutorily responsible for the RTF and this fee. (NJ Division of Taxation - Property Sale Realty Transfer Fee; source)
  • Partial exemption rates apply to qualifying senior citizens (age 62 or older), blind or disabled sellers, and low/moderate income housing, claimed on Form RTF-1. (NJ Division of Taxation - Realty Transfer Fees FAQ; source)
  • The senior/blind/disabled partial exemption is personal: it cannot be given to a decedent's estate or to a trust. (NJ Division of Taxation - Realty Transfer Fees FAQ; source)
  • Example from DOR FAQ: consideration of $325,000 with no exemption gives an RTF of $1,910. (NJ Division of Taxation - Realty Transfer Fees FAQ; source)

Who pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee?

The seller pays it. The Division of Taxation describes the Realty Transfer Fee (RTF) as a state charge on the seller for recording a deed, and the Division's rate page places the supplemental percent fee on the seller as well. It reaches every conveyance of title to New Jersey real property unless the deed or the transfer fits a listed exemption.

The amount is figured on the consideration written in the deed. In some cases the Division instead takes the assessed value of the property and divides it by the Director's Ratio for the municipality. That ratio comes from the certification of the Table of Equalized Valuations, and the Division directs filers to use the prior year's certification for a deed dated in a given year.

Anyone claiming a full or partial exemption must file Form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, with the deed. For a sheriff's sale, the applicant also files Form RTF-8, which lists other mortgagees and liens. The Division is clear that RTF-8 is not an exemption.

What are the standard transfer fee rates?

The fee is charged per $500 of consideration in brackets, and the rate depends on whether the total price is above or below $350,000. A price of $325,000 with no exemption produces a fee of $1,910, which is the Division's own worked example.

Standard seller rates when total consideration is $350,000 or less
Consideration bracketRate per $500
$0 to $150,000$2.00
$150,000 to $200,000$3.35
$200,000 to $350,000$3.90

Source: NJ Division of Taxation, Realty Transfer Fee rate schedule.

When the total consideration is over $350,000, a steeper schedule applies to the whole price:

  • $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000.
  • $4.25 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000.
  • $4.80 per $500 from $200,000 to $550,000.
  • $5.30 per $500 from $550,000 to $850,000.
  • $5.80 per $500 from $850,000 to $1,000,000, then $6.05 per $500 above $1,000,000.

Running that schedule on a $450,000 sale gives $870 on the first bracket, $425 on the second and $2,400 on the third, for a total of $3,695.

What is the extra percent fee on sales over $1 million?

The Graduated Percent Fee, often called the mansion tax, applies when the consideration is more than $1,000,000. It is charged on the total price, and the percentage climbs with the bracket. The Division's rate page states that the seller is statutorily responsible for it along with the RTF.

  • 1 percent for a price above $1 million up to $2 million.
  • 2 percent above $2 million up to $2.5 million.
  • 2.5 percent above $2.5 million up to $3 million.
  • 3 percent above $3 million up to $3.5 million.
  • 3.5 percent above $3.5 million.

The fee covers deeds for Class 2 residential property, Class 3A farms that contain a building suited for residential use, Class 4A commercial property other than industrial or apartment, and Class 4C cooperative units. Exemptions are claimed on Form RTF-1EE, which goes with every deed over $1 million and every commercial transfer.

Which deeds are exempt from the realty transfer fee?

The Division lists a set of deeds that owe no RTF. Exemptions are read narrowly, so a transfer that is not on the list pays the fee even when the reason for it seems sympathetic.

  • A deed for consideration under $100.
  • A deed between husband and wife, or between parent and child.
  • A deed from an executor or administrator to a devisee or heir to distribute the estate under the will or the intestacy laws.
  • A deed filed in the three months after a divorce decree ends the marriage of grantor and grantee.
  • A deed that gives or releases security for a debt, or that confirms or corrects a deed already recorded.
  • A deed on partition, on a sale for delinquent taxes, or by a receiver, bankruptcy trustee or assignee for creditors.

How do family sales, estates and trusts work?

Family cases produce most of the questions the Division has answered in public. A sale from parents to their daughter and son-in-law is exempt as parent to child. A father selling to his daughter and her live-in boyfriend gets an exemption on half of the price, and the other half is taxed. A legally adopted child counts as a child, but a stepchild does not unless the stepparent adopted him or her.

An executor who sells to an heir named in the will, or an heir under the intestacy rules, is exempt. A sale to anyone else is not. If a will tells the executor to sell and divide the money, the Division treats the bequest as a gift of money, so that sale pays the fee. Placing a house in trust for children is also taxable because the grantor gives up the benefits of ownership.

A divorce settlement that is simply folded into a judgment does not qualify as specific performance of a final judgment. The deed has to follow the decree closely, within the 90-day window, to use the divorce exemption. Attorney-prepared deeds in quitclaim form that move a freehold interest are treated by the Division as taxable transfers.

What reduced rates exist for seniors and disabled sellers?

Sellers age 62 or older, blind or disabled sellers, and low and moderate income housing transfers qualify for lower partial rates. For a total price of $350,000 or less, the rate is $0.50 per $500 up to $150,000 and $1.25 per $500 from $150,000 to $350,000. The Division's example is a $280,000 sale by a qualifying senior, which comes to $475.

For a total price over $350,000, the partial rates run from $1.40 per $500 on the first $150,000 up to $3.40 per $500 above $1,000,000. The claim is made on a notarized Form RTF-1 that is recorded with the deed.

The senior, blind and disabled rate is personal to the seller. A decedent's estate, a trust or a company cannot use it, and a senior who moves a house into a trust loses it. On a farm sale, only the share of the price tied to the residence and the land needed to enjoy it qualifies, usually the Class 3A portion.

Where is the fee paid, and what if the deed goes to the wrong county?

Payment goes to the county recording officer at the counter. The land's own county is the only valid place to file. A deed that lands in a different county must be filed again in the right one, with a State refund request on Form RTF-3, and the county portion has to be reclaimed from the wrong county's recording office.

Ask the county clerk for the current recording charges, because those are county fees and sit on top of the state fee. Find the RTF line on the seller's closing statement and ask whoever runs your closing how it will reach the recording officer.

More questions about New Jersey Real Estate Transfer Tax

Is the realty transfer fee paid by the buyer or the seller?

The seller pays it. The Division of Taxation describes the RTF as imposed on the seller for recording the deed, and its rate page places the Graduated Percent Fee on the seller too.

How much is the fee on a $325,000 sale?

The fee is $1,910 with no exemption. That is the Division's own example, using $2.00 per $500 to $150,000, $3.35 per $500 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 above that.

Is a sale between a parent and a child exempt?

Yes, a deed between parent and child is exempt, and that includes a legally adopted child. A stepchild relationship does not qualify unless the stepparent adopted the child.

Does the senior citizen rate work if my house is in a trust?

No. The reduced rate is a personal exemption and a trust cannot use it. A senior who deeds the house to a trust and later sells through it pays the standard rates.

What form do I file to claim an exemption?

File Form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, with the deed. It must be notarized for a partial exemption. Deeds priced above $1,000,000 also carry Form RTF-1EE for the percent fee.

What the official sources say

  • The writ of execution instructs the county sheriff to sell the property at public auction. (Foreclosure Self-Help | NJ Courts; source)
  • The sheriff has 150 days from the writ of execution to auction the property. (Foreclosure Self-Help | NJ Courts; source)
  • A completed Affidavit of Consideration for Sheriff's Deeds (RTF-8) must be supplied to the sheriff when application is made for the sale; it is not an exemption from the Realty Transfer Fee. (NJ Division of Taxation - Property Sale Realty Transfer Fee; source)
  • Debtor has 10 days after the sale to redeem; surplus proceeds beyond the mortgage debt return to the debtor. (Foreclosure Self-Help | NJ Courts; source)
  • New Jersey is a judicial foreclosure state: actions must go through the court, handled by the Office of Foreclosure and Superior Court General Equity judges. (Foreclosure Self-Help | NJ Courts; source)
  • The sheriff has 150 days from the writ of execution to auction the property; the debtor and lender may each request two stays, and a fifth is possible if both request it. (Foreclosure Self-Help | NJ Courts; source)
  • Filing fees: complaint $405, answer or first appearance $175, motion $50. (Foreclosure Self-Help | NJ Courts; source)

What is a sheriff sale in New Jersey?

A sheriff sale is the public auction that ends a New Jersey mortgage foreclosure. The Superior Court issues a writ of execution after final judgment, and that writ tells the county sheriff to sell the home to the highest bidder. The NJ Courts foreclosure page calls New Jersey a judicial foreclosure state, so every case runs through the Office of Foreclosure or a Superior Court General Equity judge.

Each county sheriff runs its own sales calendar, bidder rules and check-in routine. Morris County, Somerset County and Gloucester County all post their own terms, and the details differ from one county to the next. Ask the sheriff's sales unit in the county where the house sits for the current schedule before you plan around a date.

What has to happen before the sheriff can sell a New Jersey house?

The sheriff cannot list a home until the lender has finished several steps in court. According to the Judiciary's own description, the sequence runs like this:

  • The lender sends a Notice of Intent to Foreclose. The homeowner has 30 days from receipt to pay off the debt or reach another arrangement, and may ask for mediation.
  • The lender files a complaint, and the homeowner has 35 days to answer. No answer within 35 days makes the case uncontested.
  • Before asking for default, the lender gives a final chance to cure 14 days ahead. The homeowner then has 10 days to respond and 45 days to cure or work something out.
  • If the debt is not cured, the court enters final judgment and issues the writ of execution.

The notice of intent must also say that the homeowner can sell or transfer title. That line matters if you would rather sell the house than watch it go to auction.

How long can a New Jersey sheriff sale be delayed?

The sheriff has 150 days from the writ of execution to auction the property. Inside that window the borrower and the lender may each ask for two stays, and a fifth is possible if both sides request it. In some cases a defendant can ask for one more stay to pursue mediation.

County rules add practical detail. Gloucester County says each side gets two adjournments per foreclosure docket, with a written confirmation and a new sale date for the defendant. Morris County takes a Request for Statutory Adjournment form and requires it before noon on the scheduled sale day. A bankruptcy filing generally triggers an automatic stay, and the foreclosure resumes where it stopped once that case is resolved, according to the Judiciary's foreclosure FAQ. The sheriff must also advertise the sale for at least four weeks before holding it.

How do bidders buy at a New Jersey sheriff sale?

Bidding is an open outcry auction with no sealed bids, and the property goes to the highest bidder. The county pages open for this guide agree on the money terms. The winner pays at least 20 percent of the bid at the close of the sale, and the balance is due within 30 days. Interest runs on the balance from the 11th day after the sale, and extra time to arrange a mortgage is not granted.

Opening bids differ by county. Somerset County says the plaintiff opens at $1,000 and later bids rise in multiples of at least $1,000. Morris County and Gloucester County list a minimum bid of $100. Somerset no longer accepts cash for deposits or balances, Morris sets a $1,000 cash limit unless the sheriff approves more, and Gloucester requires a bidder registration form emailed by noon on the Tuesday before the sale.

  • A buyer gets a sheriff's deed once the full balance is paid, and the deed may not carry clear title.
  • Tax, sewer and water liens can follow the property, so the counties urge a title search before bidding.
  • Sales are subject to restrictions of record and to the rights of occupants or tenants.
  • No one may walk through the house beforehand, because the owner has no duty to allow an inspection.

Morris County also describes the Community Wealth Preservation Program. After an August 28, 2025 court order in MER-C-94-24, its right of refusal goes only to defendants, next of kin or tenants, and qualifying participants pay a 3.5 percent deposit.

Can the owner get the house back after the sale?

Yes, for a short time. The homeowner has 10 days after the auction to redeem, which the Judiciary explains as buying the property back or selling it. A successful redemption returns the bidder's deposit. Gloucester County adds that the 10 days can be extended only by a court order, and Somerset County notes that a bankruptcy filed in the same period puts the sale on hold until the court rules.

If nobody redeems, the sale proceeds first pay off the mortgage. Any amount left over returns to the homeowner. When the proceeds fall short, the lender can sue the homeowner for the remaining balance. A homeowner who suspects money is owed after the sale should ask the sheriff and the court clerk about surplus funds, and should be careful with anyone who offers to chase that money for a fee. Gloucester County links a Consumer Affairs fact sheet on surplus funds scams from its sheriff's sale page.

What happens to the people living in the house after a sheriff sale?

Occupants usually stay until some time after the auction. The lender's side must ask the court for a Writ of Possession, which instructs the sheriff to remove anyone still inside, and the sheriff tells the defendant the date to leave. Gloucester County stresses that a winning bidder has no right to enter until the deed is executed and a signed writ of possession is in hand.

Renters get separate protection. The Judiciary says a residential tenant with a valid lease in good standing is not forced to move because of foreclosure, and the buyer at the sheriff sale takes the building subject to the tenant's rights. The state's anti-eviction statute, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12, is the law the court points to. A tenant served with a foreclosure complaint should speak to an attorney and can give the lender's lawyer a copy of the lease.

What paperwork and fees come with a sheriff's deed?

Two state forms show up in this process. When the sale is requested, a completed Affidavit of Consideration for Sheriff's Deeds, Form RTF-8, goes to the sheriff. It lists other mortgagees and the balance of prior mortgages and liens, and the Division of Taxation states that it is not an exemption from the Realty Transfer Fee. The second item is the gross income tax withholding form used for deed recording. The Division says only sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales are excused from signing the seller forms GIT/REP-1, -2 or -3.

The buyer records the deed with the county clerk and pays those recording fees. Court costs for the foreclosure itself are a lender matter, and the Judiciary lists them as $405 for a complaint, $175 for an answer or first appearance and $50 for a motion.

What can a New Jersey owner do instead of waiting for the sale?

Options exist before and after judgment. A homeowner can reinstate the missed payments, pay the judgment, take a new loan, or sell. New Jersey offers free foreclosure mediation, and the Judiciary advises asking for it as early as possible after receiving the foreclosure notice. Where a case qualifies, the court also allows one extra stay of the sale for mediation.

Be wary of anyone promising a loan modification or foreclosure rescue. The Judiciary names these as scams spreading across New Jersey and recommends a free HUD and NJHMFA certified housing counselor. Because the owner keeps the right to sell until the auction, a quick sale to a buyer who pays off the lender from proceeds can end the case without a sheriff's deed. Ask the lender's attorney for a written payoff figure before you set a closing date.

More questions about New Jersey Sheriff Sales

How many days does a New Jersey homeowner have to redeem after a sheriff sale?

Ten days. The 10 days start with the auction, and the owner can buy the house back or sell it in that window. County sheriffs say only a court order can extend the period.

Does a New Jersey sheriff sale buyer have to pay all cash?

No. The winner pays at least 20 percent when the sale ends and the rest within 30 days, but counties do not grant extra time for a mortgage. Most sheriffs require certified funds, and some set a cash limit or ban cash.

Can a tenant be thrown out after a sheriff sale in New Jersey?

Not on the sale date alone. The NJ Courts say a tenant with a valid lease in good standing keeps tenant rights, and the buyer takes the building subject to them. Removal of an owner occupant needs a Writ of Possession.

Who gets the money left over from a New Jersey sheriff sale?

The homeowner receives what remains after the mortgage debt is paid. If the proceeds do not cover the debt, the lender can sue for the difference.

How long does a sheriff have to sell a house after the writ of execution?

The sheriff has 150 days from the writ. Each side may request two stays and a fifth is possible if both agree, so the real timeline can run longer than the sale date first advertised.

What the official sources say

  • A landlord must first file a landlord-tenant complaint in the Special Civil Part of Superior Court and obtain a judgment for possession before any officer may evict a residential tenant. (Landlord/Tenant | NJ Courts; source)
  • Trial date is at least 21 days from service of the summons. (Landlord/Tenant | NJ Courts; source)
  • Landlord must apply for the warrant within 30 days of the judgment, and have it executed within 30 days of issuance, unless stayed. (Landlord/Tenant | NJ Courts; source)
  • For nonpayment, a residential tenant who pays all rent due plus costs before or on the hearing date, or within three business days after eviction, has the case dismissed. (Landlord/Tenant | NJ Courts; source)
  • A landlord cannot evict without a judgment for possession and warrant of removal, so a buyer taking a tenant-occupied property cannot self-help evict. (Landlord/Tenant | NJ Courts; source)
  • Tenants served in a foreclosure should consult an attorney and may give the lender's attorney a copy of the lease; the court provides a Notice to Residential Tenants of Rights During Foreclosure. (Foreclosure Self-Help | NJ Courts; source)

How does an eviction work in New Jersey from complaint to removal?

A landlord files a landlord-tenant complaint in the Special Civil Part of the Superior Court, wins a judgment for possession, then asks the court for a warrant of removal that a court officer carries out. No one else can lawfully put a residential tenant out, and the NJ Courts landlord-tenant page says any other attempt is illegal.

The case is heard in the county courthouse where the rental sits. A landlord who is a corporation, LLC or limited partnership must be represented by a New Jersey attorney. A sole proprietor or general partnership may file without one, though the court calls a lawyer a good idea.

The whole sequence usually takes longer than the statutory minimums suggest, since the tenant can ask for settlement time, a hardship stay or a later hearing. A house sale scheduled around an occupied rental should leave room for that.

What are the steps, fees and waiting periods?

The table lays out the court-set steps and the numbers published by NJ Courts.

Special Civil Part steps and timing, from the NJ Courts landlord-tenant self-help page
StepWhat the court page says
Filing the complaint$50 for one defendant, $5 for each added defendant, plus a $7 service fee
Trial dateAt least 21 days after the summons is served
Judgment for possessionTenant has three business days to pay rent and approved costs and stop the eviction
Warrant of removal$35 plus mileage; cannot issue until three business days after judgment
Notice to leaveResidential tenant gets at least three business days after the warrant is served
Landlord deadlinesApply for the warrant within 30 days of judgment; execute it within 30 days of issuance unless stayed

The officer's own eviction fee may not exceed $75, according to the same page, and the landlord pays that and any second mileage fee directly.

What does a landlord have to file with the complaint?

The packet is longer than many owners expect. The NJ Courts kit asks for the verified complaint, a tenancy summons, and a Landlord Case Information Statement, plus a copy of the lease.

  • Lease provisions that treat fees and charges as additional rent, and any rental assistance notice or eviction-ground clauses.
  • A Registration Statement and a Certification of Lease and Registration Statement, unless the property is exempt under N.J.S.A. 46:8-27.
  • For any case other than unpaid rent, every notice sent to the tenant or housing authority that will be used at trial.

The court page explains the registration rule. A landlord who lives on the property with three units or fewer registers with the municipal Community Development Authority, while other rentals register with the state Bureau of Housing Inspection. A missing registration can become a defense.

What happens at the trial date?

Both sides must show up. If the landlord does not appear, the case is dismissed, and if the tenant does not appear, the court marks the case as a default and the landlord can apply for judgment.

When both appear, trained court staff first try to settle the matter. A settlement might give the tenant more time to move or set a payment plan, and a judge must review and approve it for residential cases involving a tenant without a lawyer. If there is no deal, the judge hears the case and either grants or denies a judgment for possession.

The tenant cannot answer in writing. The court page says the defendant must come in person, and witnesses must testify live because signed statements are not accepted.

How can a tenant stop or delay an eviction?

The court lists several tools, and each one can change a seller's timeline.

  • Pay in full: in a nonpayment case the tenant can pay all rent plus allowed costs before or at trial, or up to three business days after the eviction, and the landlord must accept it. The page notes a $500 penalty if a landlord refuses or fails to tell the court.
  • Orderly removal: an order giving up to seven more calendar days to move.
  • Hardship stay: up to six months, but only if the tenant pays everything owed and keeps paying rent during the stay.
  • Vacate the judgment: a request the court says is not granted often.

The FAQ section on the same page adds that the orderly removal and hardship requests must be made within 10 days of the eviction date. Payment from a charity or rental assistance program must also be accepted by the landlord.

What defenses can a tenant raise?

New Jersey courts hear several common defenses, and each can stall a sale plan that assumes a quick removal. The NJ Courts site lists them.

  • Habitability: the Marini Doctrine lets a tenant withhold rent over problems like no heat or hot water, mold, rodents or a broken toilet, but only by depositing rent with the court and showing the landlord had a chance to fix it. It cannot excuse late payment patterns or noise violations.
  • Unregistered rental: no registration statement can sink the filing.
  • Illegal tenancy: a condemned property or an unapproved extra unit.
  • Abatement: the judge can reduce rent owed because of a defect.
  • Subsidy notice: a landlord must tell any public agency paying part of the rent, and the case can be dismissed if it did not.

What counts as an illegal lockout in New Jersey?

Any removal without a judgment for possession and a warrant carried out by a Special Civil Part officer. The court page names changing the locks, padlocking the doors, and shutting off gas, water or electricity as illegal ways to force a tenant out.

A landlord also cannot hold a tenant's furniture or belongings to force payment. A locked-out tenant can file in the Special Civil Part asking to be let back in and for damages.

This matters to anyone buying a rented house. A buyer who closes on an occupied property cannot clear it by self-help, and the same court process runs under the new owner's name. Back rent is a separate matter, since a judgment for possession does not award the unpaid amount and the landlord must sue for it in the special civil or small claims section.

How are renters treated when the house is in foreclosure or sold at sheriff's sale?

A tenant with a valid lease who is in good standing is generally not forced out because of foreclosure. The NJ Courts foreclosure self-help page points renters to the Anti-Eviction statute, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12, and tells them to consult an attorney if served with a complaint and to give the lender's attorney a copy of the lease.

The landlord-tenant page says the purchaser at a sheriff's sale takes the building subject to tenants' rights. Tenants should also receive the court's Notice to Residential Tenants of Rights During Foreclosure.

The foreclosure page describes how the court process runs: a 30-day notice of intent, a 35-day window to answer a complaint, and a sheriff's sale that must happen within 150 days of the writ of execution. After the sale the debtor has 10 days to redeem. An owner with a tenant in the house and a mortgage in trouble can use that period to arrange a sale instead.

What are the options for selling a New Jersey house that has a tenant?

There are three practical routes. Which one fits depends on the lease, the number of units and whether the tenant cooperates.

  • Sell with the tenant in place: the buyer takes over the tenancy, and the security deposit information must be updated in writing after a transfer.
  • Negotiate a move-out: a written agreement with the tenant, ideally reviewed by the court if a case is pending.
  • Use a recognized ground: a building of three units or fewer can be cleared for an owner or buyer who will live there, after two months' notice and once the lease ends.

After the tenant leaves, personal property left behind falls under New Jersey's abandoned property statute, which the court page says a landlord should check with an attorney before handling.

More questions about New Jersey Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Can a New Jersey landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. Changing locks, padlocking doors or cutting off utilities is an illegal lockout. Only a Special Civil Part officer can carry out an eviction, and only after a judgment for possession and a warrant of removal.

How long after a judgment does a tenant have to move out in New Jersey?

At least three business days after the warrant of removal is served. The warrant itself cannot issue until three business days after the judgment, so the minimum from judgment to eviction is about a week of business days.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the back rent?

Yes, in nonpayment cases. Paying all rent due plus approved costs before or on the hearing date, or within three business days after the eviction, leads to dismissal, and the landlord must accept cash, a cashier's check or a money order.

Does a foreclosure automatically end a tenant's lease in New Jersey?

No. According to NJ Courts, a tenant with a valid lease in good standing is not forced to move just because the property is in foreclosure, and the sheriff's sale buyer takes the building subject to the tenant's rights.

Do I need a lawyer to evict a tenant in New Jersey?

Only if the landlord is a corporation, LLC or limited partnership. Individual owners and sole proprietors can file on their own, but the court recommends getting a lawyer if you can.

What the official sources say

Selling in New Jersey?

What actually gets sold at a New Jersey tax sale?

A bidder buys a lien certificate, and the owner keeps the deed. The state's Division of Local Government Services explains that title to a delinquent property is not auctioned. The certificate is a claim against the property for the unpaid tax, and it stays there until the owner redeems it or a Superior Court judgment ends the right to redeem.

A municipality that has delinquent property taxes or other municipal charges must hold at least one tax sale a year. Each town runs its own calendar, so call the municipal tax collector in the town where the house sits to learn when the next sale is set.

The lien builds up through four installment dates: February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. An unpaid balance can draw interest of up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 and up to 18 percent on anything above that. When the delinquency passes $10,000 at the end of the municipal fiscal year, the town may add a penalty of up to 6 percent.

How does bidding work, and who holds the extra money?

Bidders compete to take the lowest interest rate, and the winner is the one who accepts the least. The auction starts at the top rate allowed and bids go down. If bidding reaches the floor of one percent, bidders then offer a cash premium, starting at zero, and the highest premium wins.

The premium does not pay down your taxes. The municipality keeps it on deposit, and under R.S. 54:5-33 as amended in 2024 it goes back to the certificate holder when the owner redeems. If nobody redeems or forecloses within five years of the sale, the premium becomes municipal money.

  • The winning bidder pays the town the back taxes and interest at the close of the sale.
  • The holder should record the certificate in the county clerk's deed room within 90 days.
  • Taxes keep accruing after the sale, and a holder may pay them and earn the rate the municipality sets.
  • A later certificate on the same house ranks ahead of the earlier one.

How long before a certificate holder can start a foreclosure?

A town that bought its own certificate can sue after six months. Anyone else who holds a certificate must wait two years from the sale date. Once a suit is filed, the right to redeem continues until the court's judgment bars it.

An abandoned property follows a faster path. A holder of a certificate on a property that meets the state's abandoned property definition may file at any time, with a certification from the public officer or tax collector, or with sworn professional evidence if that certification was refused.

What does it cost to redeem a certificate?

The cost is the tax, the certificate interest, and a redemption penalty of 2, 4 or 6 percent that depends on the size of the certificate. Fees stack on top once a private holder starts the legal process, so the figure grows the longer the lien sits.

A private holder who wants search and counsel fees must first mail the owner a written notice by certified mail at least 30 days before filing the complaint. That notice has to state the redemption amount and tell the owner about the right to ask for a judicial sale. Before the complaint is filed, the holder may add only a few items:

  • A title or foreclosure search fee of no more than $350.
  • Reasonable attorney fees of no more than $150.
  • Postage and certified mailing costs for the notice.
  • A calculation fee the town charges, which an ordinance may cap at $50.

After the complaint is on file, the attorney fee is set at $2,500 plus listed expenses such as court filing fees, service of process, a title search up to $350, publication and sheriff's fees. Redemption then happens only inside that court case, and the court may direct payment to the tax collector at the municipal office.

Can an owner keep the equity if a certificate is foreclosed?

Yes, but only by asking in writing before the final judgment. Under P.L. 2024, c.39, the owner or the owner's heirs may send the Superior Court a written demand that the property go to a judicial sale or a sheriff's internet auction instead of passing straight to the certificate holder.

The amount the sale brings is treated as the property's market value. If nobody bids, the law presumes there was no equity. The sheriff deposits any surplus with the clerk of the Superior Court, and the owner claims it by motion. If the owner made the demand, the certificate holder gets a first lien on 10 percent of the surplus, capped at $5,000, for administrative costs.

Without a timely demand, the holder can foreclose with no sale, and the owner has no claim for any equity. The summons, complaint and published notice must show this right in bold type. The abandoned property route is the exception, because that suit does not require a judicial sale.

How does a city such as Newark run its tax sales?

Newark describes two kinds. A standard tax sale covers prior years' taxes and municipal charges that remain unpaid in the current year. An accelerated tax sale covers the current year's charges that are still owed after the statutory due date of November 10. Either way, the city sells a lien certificate and the property can face foreclosure if it is not redeemed in time.

The city's Finance Department also warns that a partial payment goes to the oldest quarter first. An owner who is behind on three quarters and pays something in September sees that money applied to the first quarter's principal and interest. Owners who want a payoff figure can call the Newark tax customer service lines on weekdays.

Can selling the house before the sale or the suit solve the problem?

Often it can, because the lien is paid from the sale price at closing and the buyer receives clear title. The earlier the sale closes, the smaller the payoff, since interest, the redemption penalty and foreclosure fees all grow with time.

  • Ask the tax collector for a written redemption figure good through the expected closing date.
  • If a foreclosure complaint has been filed, expect the $2,500 attorney fee and court costs to be inside that figure.
  • Send the written demand for a judicial sale before final judgment if you want any equity protected and the sale to your own buyer cannot close first.
  • Tell your closing attorney or title company about any recorded certificate so it is paid and discharged at the table.

A deed given on a sale for delinquent taxes is listed by the Division of Taxation among deeds exempt from the realty transfer fee. An ordinary sale by the owner is not exempt, so budget for that fee on the closing statement.

More questions about New Jersey Tax Sales

Can I lose my house over a small unpaid tax bill in New Jersey?

Yes, the certificate can be foreclosed after the waiting period, which is six months for a town holder and two years for other holders. Until a judgment is entered, you can still redeem by paying the tax, interest, penalty and any allowed fees. A written demand for a judicial sale or sheriff's internet auction before final judgment protects the equity.

Who receives the premium that a bidder pays?

The municipality holds it. It goes back to the certificate holder if the owner redeems and moves into the town's funds if nobody redeems or forecloses within five years. The owner's taxes are not reduced by it.

What can a private holder add to my bill before suing?

Only a title or foreclosure search fee up to $350, attorney fees up to $150, postage and certified mailing costs, and any calculation fee the town charges. The holder must send a 30-day certified mail notice first, and the notice must state the redemption amount.

Do I have to move out after a tax sale?

No. The sale transfers a lien certificate and the owner keeps title and possession. Only a final court judgment that bars redemption changes who holds the deed.

Who do I call to find the payoff?

Call the tax collector in the municipality where the house sits and ask for a redemption figure dated to your closing day. Ask whether the certificate belongs to the town or to a private holder, because that decides the foreclosure timeline and who receives payment.

The state's Division of Local Government Services lists four installment dates, February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Unpaid amounts accrue interest, and its tax sale overview says the rate may reach 8 percent on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18 percent on anything above that.

A year-end penalty of up to 6 percent can be added when a delinquency tops $10,000 at the close of the municipal fiscal year, according to the same overview. Rates and fees can change, so ask the municipal tax collector which figures apply to your bill. The tax collector, not the county, runs the process for a house in your town.

What exactly is sold at a New Jersey tax sale?

The deed stays with the owner, and the buyer purchases a tax sale certificate, which is a lien on the property. All 566 municipalities must hold at least one tax sale a year if they have delinquent taxes or other municipal charges. Branchburg's tax office explains that the list of properties has to be prepared at least 50 days before the sale, and the notice is posted in public places and published as a legal ad.

Bidding runs downward. Millville's tax office describes opening bids at the maximum 18 percent rate, with bidders dropping the rate toward zero. At zero the bidding turns to a dollar premium, so the winner is the lowest rate or, at zero, the highest premium. When nobody bids, the municipality takes the certificate at 18 percent. The premium stays on deposit with the town for up to five years under R.S. 54:5-33 as amended in 2024, and it passes to the municipality if the lien is not redeemed or foreclosed in that time.

What stops a property from going to tax sale?

Paying before the sale date stops it. Branchburg notes that a payment goes first to interest, costs and penalties, and then to the oldest delinquent principal. Close to the sale date the office may require a bank check, because personal checks are not accepted, so call the collection office before sending money. The notice stamped "Subject to Tax Sale" on a bill means last year's unpaid amount is on the list, although the current year's balance may be unpaid too.

In Millville, charges open as of November 11 are the ones that go to sale, and the collector must prepare the list 50 days before the sale. Other towns set their own sale dates. Look for the notice on your town's website or call the tax office.

Who can redeem a New Jersey tax sale certificate?

Only a short list of people can redeem. Millville names the owner, the owner's heirs, a holder of a prior outstanding certificate, a mortgagee and a legal occupant of the property, and says they may redeem only until the right to redeem is cut off. Payment goes to the tax collector in full, by cash or certified funds.

  • The amount due is the certificate plus interest and any later taxes the lien holder paid.
  • Each later payment by the investor adds to what the owner owes, which is why the balance grows.
  • After redeeming, the owner receives the cancelled certificate and is responsible for having the lien removed at the county office.

Anyone selling a house with a certificate on it should ask the tax collector for a payoff good through the closing date, then confirm the cancellation is recorded after closing.

What does redemption cost beyond the unpaid tax?

The certificate holder earns money while the lien sits. The Division of Local Government Services says a certificate redeemed before foreclosure earns a redemption penalty of 2, 4 or 6 percent, depending on the size of the original certificate, on top of the interest rate bid at the sale. Taxes keep accruing after the sale as well. The investor may pay them, and if nobody does, a later certificate is sold at the next tax sale and ranks ahead of the earlier one.

Investors are told to record the certificate with the County Clerk within 90 days of the sale. That recording is what shows up in a title search, so a house with a certificate on it will usually be flagged before a buyer closes. The 2024 law also lets a certificate holder on an abandoned property enter after certified-mail notice to make repairs or remove hazards, and those costs can be added to the unpaid balance.

When can the lien holder foreclose?

A municipality that holds the certificate may sue to foreclose the right of redemption once six months have passed from the date of sale. Any other holder must wait two years, according to R.S. 54:5-86 as amended by P.L. 2024, c.39. Abandoned property is the exception, and a holder may file at any time. Until the Superior Court enters judgment, the right to redeem continues.

Municipality6 months after the saleR.S. 54:5-86, as amended 2024
Investor or other buyer2 years after the saleR.S. 54:5-86, as amended 2024
Any holder, abandoned propertyAny timeR.S. 54:5-86(b)

Source: P.L. 2024, c.39 on the Legislature's site.

What did P.L. 2024, c.39 change for owners?

The law was approved July 10, 2024 and covers any lien not yet foreclosed on that date. Its biggest change protects equity. In a foreclosure on a tax sale certificate, the owner or heirs may demand in writing, before final judgment, that the holder go through a judicial sale or a sheriff's internet auction, the way a mortgage is foreclosed. If no demand is made, the holder can foreclose without a sale and the owner has no claim for equity.

  • The summons and complaint must carry a bold notice of this right.
  • The sheriff pays surplus funds to the Superior Court clerk, and the owner applies for them by motion.
  • A holder that is not a municipality must give 30 days' written notice by certified mail before filing, or it cannot recover search and counsel fees.
  • Once a foreclosure complaint is filed, attorney's fees of $2,500 are added to the redemption amount, plus listed costs and a title search fee capped at $350.
  • If the owner asked for a sale, the holder takes a first lien of 10 percent of the surplus for administrative costs, up to $5,000.

How should a New Jersey owner handle a tax lien when selling the house?

Start by asking the tax collector which certificates exist and which charges remain unpaid. A buyer will expect clear title, and a redemption that includes foreclosure costs costs more than one made early. If a complaint has been filed, redemption must be made in that case, and the court can set attorney's fees and costs at any point.

A sale also gives you a way to protect equity. An owner who sells for market value and pays the redemption amount from proceeds keeps the remainder. Waiting through a foreclosure without demanding a sale can mean losing that equity. Legal Services of New Jersey runs a statewide hotline at 1-888-LSNJ-LAW for owners who cannot afford a lawyer, and Branchburg's tax office points readers to the same number.

More questions about New Jersey Tax Liens and Delinquent Property Tax

What is a tax sale certificate in New Jersey?

It is a lien sold at auction for unpaid taxes or municipal charges. The buyer does not receive the deed, but may earn interest and can foreclose if the owner never redeems.

How long do New Jersey owners have to redeem before foreclosure?

Two years when an investor holds the certificate, and six months when the municipality does. Redemption stays open until the Superior Court enters a final judgment barring it.

Can a New Jersey owner lose a house over a small tax debt?

Yes, if the certificate goes unredeemed and the holder completes a foreclosure. The 2024 law lets the owner demand a judicial sale or sheriff internet auction before final judgment to preserve equity.

Do fees get added to a tax lien in New Jersey?

Yes. After a foreclosure complaint, the redemption amount includes $2,500 in attorney's fees and listed costs, with a search fee capped at $350. Earlier notice costs are smaller.

Who do I call to get a redemption figure?

Call the municipal tax collector in the town where the house sits. Ask for a written payoff good through your planned closing date.

New Jersey Seller Disclosure Rules FAQ

Do I have to disclose problems when I sell?

See the statute cited above for what New Jersey requires.

What must a New Jersey seller disclose?

A New Jersey seller of a home must complete a property condition disclosure statement, known as the PCDS, and it must be signed. The form comes from the Division of Consumer Affairs under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-29.1(d), and the statute behind it is N.J.S.A. 56:8-19.1. P.L. 2024, c.32 made it a duty for real estate brokerage firms to obtain the signed statement from a residential seller.

A seller without an agent has the same job. The law says that a seller who is not working with a brokerage firm, or who works with a firm acting as transaction broker, must hand the statement to the buyer before the buyer becomes obligated under any contract. That timing matters. A statement delivered after the contract is signed does not meet the rule as written in section 2(e) of P.L. 2024, c.32.

Does New Jersey require a flood disclosure?

Yes. Since March 20, 2024, every seller of real property in the state must disclose flood risk information through the PCDS before the buyer is bound by a purchase contract. The Department of Environmental Protection explains two parts. The seller states whether the property is in FEMA's Special Flood Hazard Area or Moderate Flood Hazard Area, and the seller reports any actual knowledge about the property's flood risks.

The law is P.L. 2023, c.94, enacted July 3, 2023. The same page notes that sea-level rise is expected to meet or exceed 2.1 feet above 2000 levels by 2050 and that heavier rainfall raises flash flood risk inland. DEP offers a Flood Risk Notification Tool to help sellers find the zone answers. Because the duty applies to every seller, a cash sale or an as-is sale does not remove the question.

Which other New Jersey disclosures show up when you sell a house?

The Department of Banking and Insurance publishes a consumer guide that lists the items beyond the statement. Several belong to the seller, and others are mostly for the buyer to investigate.

  • Lead paint: for a house built before 1978, the seller must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards, give the buyer a lead disclosure form, and share any records or reports.
  • Material physical conditions: P.L. 2024, c.32 requires the listing brokerage to disclose existing material information about the property's physical condition that it knows or that a reasonable effort would reveal.
  • Stigmatized property: a seller and agent do not have to volunteer a haunting or a violent death, but must answer truthfully if the buyer asks.
  • Off-site conditions: municipal clerks keep lists of nearby conditions that may affect value, and buyers can review them.
  • Megan's Law: the county prosecutor decides how notice is given about convicted offenders in an area.

Mold, radon and asbestos appear in the same guide as inspection topics for the buyer, so expect questions about them during an inspection even though they are not separate seller forms.

What changed when P.L. 2024, c.32 took effect?

The law was signed July 10, 2024 and became effective August 1, 2024. The Real Estate Commission's Bulletin 24-11 explains that it adds designated agency as a fifth business relationship and requires a written brokerage services agreement in residential deals. Compensation terms in that agreement must say expressly that broker pay is negotiable and not set by law.

The Act also requires a posted sign at residential open houses warning visitors that the agent represents the seller and that information given to the agent is not confidential. A seller who lists with an agent should expect to sign the agency disclosure at the start and to hand over the PCDS soon after.

When can a New Jersey buyer or seller walk away after signing?

The Banking and Insurance guide describes an attorney review clause. When a licensee prepares the contract of sale, it must give buyer and seller three business days from delivery of the fully signed contract to consult an attorney. In that period the attorney can propose revisions or cancel the contract. If you hired an attorney to draft the contract instead, the guide says the review period may or may not be included, so ask the attorney.

This is where disclosure answers get tested. A statement that mentions flooding, a past repair or a lead history can lead the buyer's lawyer to ask for a repair credit or a price change during the review days. Answering fully at the start keeps those three days from becoming a renegotiation of surprises.

What happens after the buyer's inspection in New Jersey?

The state's buyer guide recommends an independent home inspection soon after a contract becomes binding, with the buyer present. The inspector reports on the structure, construction and mechanical systems and flags defects or items to replace. If the report shows problems, buyer and seller are held to the time limits written in the contract for delivering the report and for the seller to decide whether to correct the items.

For a seller, the practical point is to read those inspection and response deadlines before signing. Missing the contract's response window can leave you without a say in how a repair issue gets resolved. The guide tells buyers to consult an agent or attorney for the specifics of their contract, and sellers can do the same.

What seller taxes and forms come at a New Jersey closing?

The seller pays the Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. The Division of Taxation calculates it from the consideration in the deed, using a rate per $500 that rises with price. For a deal of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 from $200,000 to $350,000. An Affidavit of Consideration, Form RTF-1, claims any exemption. Sales above $1,000,000 also carry a graduated percent fee that starts at 1 percent of consideration.

A GIT/REP form is also recorded with the deed. New Jersey resident individuals, estates and trusts sign the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax unless an assurance on that form applies, and the payment cannot be less than 2 percent of the total consideration in the deed. Executors and trustees complete the form for the estate or trust.

Can a seller in foreclosure still sell the house?

Yes. The NJ Courts say the Notice of Intent to Foreclose must state that the debtor can sell or transfer the title. After a sheriff sale the owner also has 10 days to redeem by buying back or selling. Disclosure rules still apply to a distressed sale, so the PCDS, flood answers and any lead form go to the buyer the same way.

The Judiciary also warns about foreclosure rescue and loan modification scams and recommends a free HUD and NJHMFA certified housing counselor. Anyone who asks for an upfront fee to save a home deserves a second look before you sign.

More questions about New Jersey Seller Disclosure Rules When Selling a House

Is the property condition disclosure statement required for every New Jersey home sale?

For residential sales, yes. A licensee must obtain the signed statement from the seller, and a seller without an agent must give it to the buyer before the buyer is bound by the contract.

Do I have to disclose that my New Jersey house floods?

Yes, to the extent you know. Every seller must state whether the property is in a FEMA Special or Moderate Flood Hazard Area and report actual knowledge of flood risk before the buyer is obligated.

Is lead paint disclosure required in New Jersey?

Yes for houses built before 1978. The seller discloses known lead-based paint and hazards, provides the lead disclosure form and passes along any records or reports in hand.

Must a New Jersey seller disclose a death in the house?

Not unless asked. Stigmatized property, such as a violent death, does not have to be volunteered, but a seller or agent who knows the answer must give it truthfully when a buyer asks.

Who pays the realty transfer fee in New Jersey?

The seller pays it. The Division of Taxation sets rates per $500 of consideration, and the fee is collected when the deed is recorded with the county clerk.
